passage: After the branch shutters came down, Jahnavi knocked on Rafiq's cabin with a sheet of paper folded twice. "Sir, can I ask for something small?" Rafiq, her branch manager, waved her in. For three years she had followed exactly the plan her parents made the day she cleared the bank exam: counter, loans desk, promotion test. Last month, while training two new joiners, she had noticed she stayed late without once looking at the clock. "I'd like to run the induction sessions for new staff, alongside my desk work. Maybe for three months, to see if I'm any good." Rafiq read her plan. "And your parents?" "I told them on Sunday. I said the job they pushed me toward gave me steady ground, and I'm grateful. I'm not quitting. I just want to see what I'd build on it." He signed the sheet. "Three months, then."

qa.q: How long had Jahnavi followed her parents' plan at the bank?
qa.a: For three years: counter, loans desk, promotion test.

qa.q: What did staying late without looking at the clock make Jahnavi think?
qa.a: It made her think she might truly enjoy training people, something she noticed for herself rather than something planned for her.

qa.q: Why was asking for a three-month trial a wise choice for Jahnavi?
qa.a: It let her test a small change without throwing away the steady job she still values, so she gets real evidence instead of a dramatic break.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi's parents have felt hearing her Sunday explanation?
qa.a: They may have felt respected and relieved, since she thanked them for the steady ground and said she wasn't quitting, so the change didn't sound like a rejection.

grounding: A young professional who sees she followed her parents' script tests a small change, keeps what she values and explains it to them with respect.

passage:
Dear Vijay bhaiya,
You'll hear from Papa soon, so I wanted you to hear it from me first. I'm not applying for the master's abroad this year.
Don't panic. I'm not leaving engineering. I still love the puzzle of code, and that part is mine, not only the dream of a father who calls me his engineer daughter. What I've realised is that I picked every step because it was the next box on his list, and I never asked what I wanted to build.
So I'm trying something small. From next month I'm moving to the team that makes attendance software for village schools. Same company, same pay. If I hate it in six months, I'll know.
I'll tell Papa on the Sunday call. I want to thank him properly first, because his push got me here, and then explain. Could you be on the call? Not to fight for me. Just so I'm not alone.
Preeti

qa.q: Which team is Preeti moving to from next month?
qa.a: The team that makes attendance software for village schools, in the same company.

qa.q: Why does Preeti want Vijay on the Sunday call?
qa.a: She feels nervous about telling Papa and wants company so she isn't alone, though she doesn't want Vijay to fight for her.

qa.q: What makes Preeti's plan a careful choice rather than a dramatic break?
qa.a: She keeps the coding she truly loves, stays in the same company and gives the new team six months, so she can learn without burning anything down.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if Preeti starts the call by thanking him?
qa.a: He may feel his effort is being honoured rather than rejected, which could make him readier to listen to her new plan.

grounding: A young professional who realises she ticked off her father's list keeps the parts she endorses, tries one small change and plans to explain it with respect.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage: Nilesh, you said the theme of your podcast this month is plans that changed. Mine didn't really change. It got edited. My life was written before I could read: the good daughter, Gurleen, will teach at Nanaji's school, marry by twenty-five, live two streets away. And I did it. I topped my B.Ed class and was back at that school by twenty-two. Then last year a Class 8 girl asked me what I had wanted to be, and I had no answer. That scared me more than any fight could. I didn't quit, and I didn't shout at my parents. I kept teaching, because the classroom turns out to be truly mine. But I asked for one year before any wedding talk, and I started a free evening reading club in our mohalla that nobody planned for me. When I explained it to Mummy, I said, "You gave me the ground. Let me choose some of what grows on it."

qa.q: What did the Class 8 girl ask Gurleen?
qa.a: She asked Gurleen what she had wanted to be.

qa.q: Why did the girl's question scare Gurleen more than a fight could?
qa.a: Having no answer made Gurleen feel she had lived a script written for her without ever choosing it herself.

qa.q: Which choices show Gurleen changing course without burning everything down?
qa.a: She kept teaching because it is truly hers, asked for one year before wedding talk and started the evening reading club, testing small changes instead of quitting.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's Mummy hear the line about the ground and what grows on it?
qa.a: She may hear respect for what the family gave rather than rejection, which makes it easier to accept Gurleen's own choices.

grounding: A young teacher who notices her life followed a family script keeps the teaching she endorses, makes small new choices and explains them respectfully.

passage:
I'm Ritu, Kalyani's younger sister, so I've watched this from the sofa. For three years she did exactly what Papa planned: dental college, then the chair next to his in the family clinic. She never complained. She also stopped humming.
Last spring something shifted, though I can't say what went on inside her. She didn't quit or shout. She asked Papa if she could take Saturdays off to teach a children's dance class, just for three months, and she started taking all the clinic's child patients herself, because, she said, she likes making scared kids laugh.
At dinner she explained it carefully. "Papa, I'm keeping dentistry. I'm choosing the parts I love, and I want one day that's only mine." Papa was quiet, then passed her the dal. The humming came back.

qa.q: What did Kalyani ask to take off to teach a children's dance class?
qa.a: She asked to take Saturdays off, just for three months.

qa.q: What might the return of Kalyani's humming suggest, even though Ritu can't be sure what she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels lighter and more like herself now that part of her life is chosen by her.

qa.q: Which choice of Kalyani's avoided both blaming Papa and burning everything down?
qa.a: She kept dentistry, tested one small change with Saturdays, kept the child patients she loves, and explained it to Papa with respect.

qa.q: What might Papa be feeling when he goes quiet and then passes the dal?
qa.a: He may feel surprised or a little hurt at first, but passing the dal suggests he accepts her choice and still feels close to her.

grounding: A sister describes a young dentist who realises she followed her father's script and responds with small tested changes, keeping what she values and explaining respectfully.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage:
Saturday. At his cousin's wedding an uncle asked Dhruv, twenty-five, about his plans. He heard himself recite them: an MBA next year, then take over the steel yard, like Papa. Every sentence was Papa's. Driving home he felt oddly hollow, and he didn't want to blame anyone for it.
Two weeks later. He didn't resign or apply abroad. He asked his father, Manoj, whether he could run the scrap-recycling pilot at the yard for six months, the one idea at work that kept him awake in a good way. He also joined a Sunday woodworking class, just to see.
A month later. Over breakfast he told Papa, "I'm staying in the business, but I want to choose my part of it. I'll decide about the MBA after the pilot." Manoj lowered his newspaper. "You've been thinking." "I have. You taught me to plan. I'm planning."

qa.q: What pilot did Dhruv ask to run at the yard?
qa.a: The scrap-recycling pilot, for six months.

qa.q: What did Dhruv feel driving home from the wedding, and why?
qa.a: He felt hollow and unsettled because he realised every sentence of his plan was his father's, not his own.

qa.q: What made Dhruv's response wiser than resigning or simply carrying on?
qa.a: He tested small changes, the pilot and the woodworking class, before deciding, keeping the business he values while choosing his own part of it.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel hearing 'You taught me to plan. I'm planning'?
qa.a: He may feel respected rather than rejected, since Dhruv frames the change as using what his father taught him.

grounding: Over a month a young man notices he has been reciting his father's plan and responds with small tested changes, keeping what he values and explaining with respect.
